跟着山田商事营业部的王さん，练接电话、拜访客户、开会、报联商、处理投诉、谈判、面: Follow Wang from the Sales Department at Yamada Shoji and practice business situations: answering the phone, visiting clients, meetings, 「報連相」 (reporting, keeping others informed and consulting), handling complaints, negotiating, job interviews, entertaining clients, and more.
早会上的自我介绍: Introducing yourself at the morning meeting
四月第一个周一早上九点，山田商事营业部开早会。田中课长先向大家宣布有新同事加入，: It's 9 a.m. on the first Monday in April, and the Sales Department at Yamada Shoji is holding its morning meeting. Section Chief Tanaka first announces to everyone that a new colleague is joining, then asks Wang to come up to the front. In about a minute, Wang has to cover his department, his name, his background and his resolve, and finish with a bow. The section chief then announces who will be training him and gives the day's meeting notice.
营业部课长，五十岁左右，话不多，对新人要求严但很照顾: Section chief in the Sales Department, around fifty; a man of few words who is strict with new employees but looks out for them
上海人，在日本读完大学后入职山田商事营业部的新员工: From Shanghai; a new employee who joined the Sales Department at Yamada Shoji after finishing university in Japan
营业部入职五六年的前辈，亲切开朗，负责带王さん: Senior colleague who has been in the Sales Department for five or six years; friendly and cheerful, and in charge of training Wang
早会上王さん是全场资历最浅的人，面对课长和所有前辈都要用自谦语加丁宁语。课长对部: At the morning meeting, Wang is the most junior person in the room, so with the section chief and all his senior colleagues he has to use humble language (kenjōgo) on top of the polite (です/ます) style. It's perfectly normal for the section chief to use a plain-style word like 「ありがとう」 with his subordinates; that's how a superior speaks to those below him. Sato adds 「ね」 when she talks to the newcomer, which sounds fairly friendly, but Wang should still reply to her with 「よろしくお願いいたします」.
大家早上好。今天起销售部有一位新同事加入。小王，请。: Good morning, everyone. Starting today, a new member is joining the Sales Department. Wang, go ahead.
大家早上好。我叫王，从今天起被分配到销售部。: Good morning. I've been assigned to the Sales Department as of today. My name is Wang.
「本日より」比「今日から」正式，「配属になりました」说明自己被分到哪个部门，再用: 「本日より」 is more formal than 「今日から」. 「配属になりました」 tells people which department you've been assigned to, and then you give your name with 「と申します」. The section chief says 「今日から」 because he's the superior speaking among his own people; when a new employee speaks for himself, he needs to be one notch more formal.
我来自中国上海，大学专业是经营学。: I'm from Shanghai, China, and I majored in business administration at university.
这是我第一次在日本公司工作，想必会有很多不足之处，我会全力以赴，争取早日成为团队: This is my first time working at a Japanese company, so I expect I'll fall short in many ways, but I'll do my very best to become a contributing member of the team as soon as I can.
「至らない点も多いかと存じますが」是新人致辞的经典谦虚句：先承认自己不成熟，再说: 「至らない点も多いかと存じますが」 is a classic modest line in a newcomer's speech: first you admit that you're still inexperienced, then you state your resolve with 「一日も早く戦力になれるよう」. Just saying 「頑張ります」 is fine too, but if you add the first half, your listeners will feel that you know how to conduct yourself.
还请各位多多指导、多多鞭策。: I humbly ask for your guidance and encouragement.
「ご指導ご鞭撻のほど」是书面味很浓的固定说法，「鞭撻」是鞭策。日常对话几乎不用，: 「ご指導ご鞭撻のほど」 is a set phrase with a strongly literary flavor; 「鞭撻」 means spurring someone on. It's almost never used in everyday conversation, but it's very common in speeches when joining a company, transferring, or taking up a new post. Always bow after saying it, and hold the bow for a second or two before straightening up.
谢谢。小王的带教由佐藤负责。: Thank you. I've asked Sato to be Wang's trainer.
我是佐藤。有不懂的地方，尽管问我。: I'm Sato. If you don't understand something, don't hesitate to ask me anything, okay?
前辈说「遠慮なく何でも聞いてくださいね」是真心话，不是客套。新人最常犯的错是怕麻: When a senior colleague says 「遠慮なく何でも聞いてくださいね」, she means it; it's not just politeness. The most common mistake new employees make is being afraid of bothering people, so they don't ask even when they don't understand, and end up making mistakes. If someone really says this to you, go ahead and ask.
谢谢您。佐藤前辈，请多关照。: Thank you. I look forward to working with you, Sato.
下面是今天的通知事项。下午两点开全体会议，请大家到第一会议室集合。: Now, today's announcements. There's an all-hands meeting at 2 p.m., so everyone please gather in Conference Room 1.
听到上司的通知，用「承知いたしました」或「かしこまりました」回应。「了解です」在: When your boss gives you a notice, respond with 「承知いたしました」 or 「かしこまりました」. At quite a few companies, 「了解です」 is considered not polite enough toward superiors, so new employees are better off not using it.
很多日本公司每天开始工作前开，通知事项、轮流发言: Held every day before work starts at many Japanese companies, for announcements and with people taking turns to speak
「営業部に配属になる」「配属先」= 被分到的部门: 「営業部に配属になる」 (to be assigned to the Sales Department); 「配属先」 = the department one is assigned to
出生地、毕业学校: place one comes from, school one graduated from
「上海出身」「〇〇大学出身」，自我介绍必用: 「上海出身」 (from Shanghai), 「〇〇大学出身」 (a graduate of XX University); a must in self-introductions
「経営学を専攻する」，说过去的事用「専攻しておりました」: 「経営学を専攻する」 (to major in business administration); to talk about the past, use 「専攻しておりました」
只用来谦虚地说自己：「至らない点」「至らない者ですが」: Used only to speak modestly about yourself: 「至らない点」 (my shortcomings), 「至らない者ですが」 (inexperienced as I am)
能干活的力量: someone who can do real work, useful strength
「戦力になる」= 能独当一面，上司夸新人「もう戦力だね」: 「戦力になる」 = to become able to pull one's own weight; a boss might praise a new employee with 「もう戦力だね」 (you're already a real asset)
竭尽全力: with all one's might, one's very best
「精一杯頑張ります」，表决心的常用说法: 「精一杯頑張ります」 (I'll do my very best) is a common way to state your resolve
「ご指導をお願いします」，对上司、前辈用: 「ご指導をお願いします」 (please give me your guidance); used with bosses and senior colleagues
新人入职时专门带他的前辈，也叫「OJT担当」: The senior colleague assigned to look after a new employee when they join; also called 「OJT担当」 (on-the-job training supervisor)
「遠慮なく」= 别客气；「遠慮します」也可以表示委婉拒绝: 「遠慮なく」 = don't hold back, feel free; 「遠慮します」 can also be a polite way of declining
早会、会议上「今日の連絡事項です」开始传达: At morning meetings and other meetings, the announcements start with 「今日の連絡事項です」
整个部门或全公司一起开的会: A meeting held by an entire department or the whole company
「承知いたしました」是对上司、客户的正式回应: 「承知いたしました」 is the formal response to bosses and clients
从今天起被分到……，我叫……: as of today I've been assigned to ...; my name is ...
本日より + 部门 + に配属になりました + 名字 + と申します: 本日より + department + に配属になりました + name + と申します
一句话交代「什么时候、在哪个部门、我是谁」，正好是同事最想知道的。「申す」是「言: In a single sentence it tells people when, which department, and who you are, which is exactly what your coworkers most want to know. 「申す」 is the humble form of 「言う」 and lowers yourself; it's very appropriate to use with your boss and senior colleagues at your own company's morning meeting.
从今天起分到总务部，我姓李。: I've been assigned to the General Affairs Department as of today. My name is Li.
从四月起分到大阪分店，我姓陈。: I've been assigned to the Osaka branch as of April. My name is Chen.
想必有很多不足之处，但……: I expect I'll fall short in many ways, but ...
至らない点も多いかと存じますが + 决心或请求: 至らない点も多いかと存じますが + resolution or request
日本人致辞喜欢先放低自己再表决心，这样后面的「頑張ります」才不显得自大。「存じま: In speeches, Japanese people like to lower themselves first and then state their resolve, so that the 「頑張ります」 that follows doesn't sound arrogant. 「存じます」 is the humble form of 「思う」; it's more formal than 「思います」 and suits formal occasions.
想必有很多不足，请多关照。: I expect I'll fall short in many ways, but I look forward to working with you.
想必有很多不足，但我会尽全力。: I expect I'll fall short in many ways, but I'll do my very best.
接受指示、通知时直接说: Say it as is when you accept an instruction or a notice
比「わかりました」正式，对上司和客户都能用。说的时候声音清楚、干脆，再加一句具体: It's more formal than 「わかりました」 and can be used with both bosses and clients. Say it in a clear, crisp voice, and add a concrete action (for example, 「二時に参ります」); the other person will feel even more reassured.
明白了，我两点去第一会议室。: Understood. I'll be in Conference Room 1 at two.
明白了，我马上准备。: Understood. I'll get it ready right away.
入职第一天、调到新部门、新项目开会时做自我介绍都可以用这一套：部门、名字、出身、: You can use this same formula whenever you introduce yourself: on your first day at a company, after transferring to a new department, or at a new project's first meeting. Give your department, name, where you're from, your background and your resolve, then finish with 「よろしくお願いいたします」 and a bow, keeping it to about a minute.
不要讲太长，把简历从头念一遍会让大家站着发愁。也不要说「王です、よろしく」这么随: Don't go on too long; reading out your whole résumé from the start will leave everyone standing there wishing you'd finish. Don't be too casual either, as in 「王です、よろしく」. It's easy to open with an enthusiastic "Hi, everyone!" and then talk at length about your ambitions, but Japanese morning meetings favor something short and composed.
课长和前辈其实只想知道「这个人好不好相处、能不能一起干活」。简短、谦虚、声音清楚: What the section chief and your senior colleagues really want to know is "Is this person easy to get along with, and can we work together?" A short, modest self-introduction in a clear voice makes everyone think "This new employee knows how things are done, so we can teach them with confidence," and they'll be more willing to take you under their wing from then on.
日本公司的早会很短，自我介绍讲得好不好，大家记住的其实是你的态度。王さん说完「ご: Morning meetings at Japanese companies are short, and however well your self-introduction goes, what people actually remember is your attitude. The moment Wang finished 「ご指導ご鞭撻のほど」 and bowed deeply, the section chief was already grading him in his head. When your name is called, first answer 「はい」 in a loud, clear voice, look at everyone while you speak, and when you finish, bow and hold it for a second or two. These small gestures matter more than the content. One more thing: remember the name of the senior colleague who will be training you, and go say hello to them on your own that same day. When Sato says 「遠慮なく何でも聞いて」, she means it. The worst thing a new employee can do is pretend to understand when they don't. The sooner your shortcomings come out, the sooner they get corrected and the faster you grow. Don't be afraid of saying something wrong; new employees who speak up are the most welcome.
早会上第一次报自己的名字，最合适的说法是？: When you give your name for the first time at a morning meeting, which is the most appropriate way to say it?
「申す」是「言う」的自谦语，用来报自己的名字。「おっしゃる」是尊敬语，只能用在别: 「申す」 is the humble form of 「言う」 and is used to give your own name. 「おっしゃる」 is honorific and can only be used about other people; 「申し上げる」 is used when telling someone something, not for giving your name.
「ご指導ご鞭撻のほど」后面接哪一句最合适？: Which phrase best follows 「ご指導ご鞭撻のほど」?
这是新人致辞的固定结尾，后面接最郑重的「どうぞよろしくお願いいたします」。「よろ: This is the set ending of a newcomer's speech, and it's followed by the most formal phrase, 「どうぞよろしくお願いいたします」. 「よろしく頼むよ」 is how a superior talks to subordinates, and 「ご苦労様です」 can't be said to your boss either.
课长通知下午两点开全体会议，你怎么回答最合适？: The section chief announces an all-hands meeting at 2 p.m. What is the most appropriate reply?
「承知いたしました」是对上司最稳妥的回答。「了解！」「わかったよ」太随便，「ご苦: 「承知いたしました」 is the safest reply to a boss. 「了解！」 and 「わかったよ」 are too casual, and 「ご苦労様でした」 is what a superior says to thank subordinates for their efforts.
